title: IAF lands IL-76 heavy transport at Nyoma, 25 km from the LAC, in a record high-altitude landing
dek: The 13,629-ft airbase in eastern Ladakh can now take the air force's heavy-lift jets, bringing large loads closer to the frontier with China.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
An Indian Air Force IL-76MD heavy transport aircraft has landed at the Nyoma airbase in eastern Ladakh, about 25 km from the Line of Actual Control with China, in what the IAF says is the highest-altitude landing ever made by the aircraft anywhere in the world.

The IAF announced the landing on social media on Saturday. "An Indian Air Force IL-76MD has scripted history with a successful landing at Nyoma," it said, calling it a milestone that reinforces India's strategic airlift capability. The airbase, also known as Mudh-Nyoma, sits at 13,629 feet (about 4,150 metres) above sea level.

## What the landing shows

The IL-76MD is a four-engine, Russian-origin transport that the IAF uses to carry troops, vehicles and heavy equipment. Thin air at high altitude reduces engine thrust and lift, so heavy aircraft need longer runways and careful handling to land and take off safely; the IAF credited the crew's skill and precision for the landing.

A base that can take an IL-76 lets the IAF fly larger loads closer to the LAC. When the base was made operational, Air Chief Marshal A P Singh landed there in a smaller C-130J Super Hercules transport, according to reports. The IAF did not say what the aircraft carried, whether the landing was a trial or an operational flight, or how often such flights will now run.

## Background

Nyoma became operational in November last year, according to reports, and is Ladakh's fourth air base after Leh, Kargil and Thoise. It has been built to handle fighter jets, helicopters and transport aircraft. Daulat Beg Oldi, an advanced landing ground in northern Ladakh at about 16,700 feet, is regarded as the world's highest airfield, but it is used by smaller aircraft. The defence ministry is upgrading airfields and advanced landing grounds along the LAC, reports said.

Both India and China have expanded roads, bridges, airfields and troop shelters along their disputed border since the clash in the Galwan valley in June 2020, in which 20 Indian soldiers were killed. In October 2024 the two countries agreed on patrolling arrangements at Depsang and Demchok, the last two points of friction in eastern Ladakh, and disengagement there followed. Both sides still keep large forces along the frontier, and the boundary itself remains undefined.

## Why it matters

For India, faster airlift to the frontier shortens the time needed to reinforce troops in eastern Ladakh, where high passes on the road routes can be closed by snow in winter. The ability to move troops and equipment quickly has been a central concern for both armies since the 2020 stand-off, when each side rushed tens of thousands of soldiers to the border. China had not commented publicly on the Nyoma landing by Saturday evening.

## What happens next

The IAF has not announced a schedule for regular heavy-lift flights to Nyoma. Its operations in Ladakh are usually tested hardest in winter, when temperatures fall well below freezing and the passes into the region close.
